lessons.title: Organizing Your Inventory System
lessons.body:
Start by grouping your products into categories that make sense for your business. For example, if you sell phone accessories, you might have categories like chargers, earphones, phone cases, and power banks. Within each category, assign a unique code to every item. Use a simple system like 'CH-001' for charger number one. Write this code on the item's packaging with a permanent marker. This code becomes your inventory's identity.

Next, create a master inventory list. You can use a notebook, but a spreadsheet like Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel is better because it's easy to update and search. Your list should have columns for: Item Code, Item Name, Category, Quantity in Stock, Cost Price, Selling Price, and Location (e.g., Shelf A, Bin 3). Update this list every time you buy or sell. If you don't have a computer, use a dedicated notebook and keep it with your stock at all times.

Physical organization is key. Use cheap shelving units, plastic bins, or even cardboard boxes. Label every shelf and bin clearly with the category or item codes. Keep fast-moving items at eye level and slow movers on higher or lower shelves. In many African markets, space is tight, so use vertical space: stack bins, hang items on walls, and use under-bed storage if working from home.

Do a physical count every week. Compare it to your master list. If numbers don't match, investigate immediatelyâmaybe a sale wasn't recorded or an item was misplaced. This weekly check catches problems early. Also, keep a 'reorder point' for each item: when stock falls to a certain number (e.g., 10 units), it's time to buy more. This prevents stockouts.

Finally, secure your inventory. If you share space, use lockable cabinets or bins. Keep a record of who takes what. For high-value items, consider a separate locked box. A simple, consistent system saves you time, money, and stress.

lessons.title: Using Inventory Management Software
lessons.body:
When your business grows beyond a few dozen items, a spreadsheet becomes slow and error-prone. Inventory management software helps you track stock in real time, avoid overselling, and know exactly what to reorder. You don't need expensive software; many free or low-cost options work well in Africa.

Start with free tools like Zoho Inventory (free up to 50 orders/month) or Wave Inventory (free). If you sell on Jumia, Konga, or Takealot, use their seller appsâthey often include basic inventory tracking. For WhatsApp-based sales, apps like Catlog or Kudi can help. If you have a smartphone, you can also use Google Sheets with add-ons like AppSheet to create a simple mobile app for your inventory.

To set up, enter your product list with codes, quantities, and reorder points. Connect the software to your sales channels if possible. For example, if you sell on Instagram and Jumia, the software can sync stock so you don't sell an item you don't have. Train yourself: watch YouTube tutorials (search 'Zoho Inventory tutorial for beginners') and practice with dummy data.

Use the software daily. When you make a sale, record it immediately. When you receive new stock, update quantities. Set alerts for low stockâmost software can email or text you when an item hits its reorder point. This prevents the common problem of running out of your best sellers.

If you don't have reliable internet, choose software that works offline and syncs later, like Zoho Inventory's mobile app. Always back up your data weekly to Google Drive or a USB drive. Even with software, do a physical count once a month to catch errors. The goal is to spend less time counting and more time selling.

lessons.title: Storing and Packaging Supplies
lessons.body:
Proper storage protects your goods from damage, theft, and pests. In many African cities, heat, dust, and humidity are big threats. Store items in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. If you're in a humid area like Lagos or Mombasa, use silica gel packets in bins to absorb moisture. For dust, keep items in closed plastic containers or cabinets.

Choose the right containers. Clear plastic bins with lids are ideal because you can see what's inside without opening. They also stack, saving space. For smaller items like jewellery or phone cases, use compartment boxes or zip-lock bags. Label everything with a permanent marker: category, item code, and quantity. If you're storing textiles, fold them neatly and place in breathable cotton bags to prevent mildew.

Packaging supplies are just as important. When shipping to customers, use sturdy materials. For example, padded envelopes for small electronics, corrugated boxes for larger items, and bubble wrap for fragile goods. Buy these in bulk from local suppliers or online platforms like Alibaba or Jumia Business. A roll of bubble wrap costs about 5,000 Naira in Nigeria or 200 KES in Kenya and lasts for many orders.

Consider your brand image. A clean, professional package builds trust. Use branded stickers or tape if possible. Include a thank-you note. For eco-friendly options, use recycled boxes or biodegradable mailers. But always prioritise protectionâa damaged item costs you a refund and a bad review.

Organise your packing station. Keep supplies within reach: tape dispenser, scissors, labels, and a scale for weighing packages. If you work from home, designate a corner for packing. This reduces errors and speeds up order fulfilment. Finally, store empty packaging materials separately from your sellable inventory to avoid clutter and confusion.

lessons.title: Tracking Sales and Restocking
lessons.body:
Tracking sales tells you what's selling, what's not, and when to restock. Without this, you'll either run out of popular items or tie up cash in dead stock. Start by recording every saleâeven those via WhatsApp or in person. Use a simple sales log: date, item code, quantity sold, selling price, and channel (e.g., Jumia, Instagram, walk-in). A notebook works, but a spreadsheet is better because you can sum totals automatically.

At the end of each week, review your sales. Identify your top 5 sellers and your slow movers. For top sellers, check if you have enough stock to last until your next restock. If not, order more immediately. For slow movers, consider promotions or bundling. Calculate your sales velocity: how many units of an item do you sell per week on average? For example, if you sell 20 phone chargers per week, and your supplier takes 2 weeks to deliver, you need to reorder when stock hits 40 units (plus a safety buffer of 10).

Set reorder points for every item. This is the minimum stock level that triggers a new order. Use the formula: Reorder Point = (Average Daily Sales Ã Lead Time in Days) + Safety Stock. If you sell 3 units per day and lead time is 7 days, with 5 units safety stock, reorder at 26 units. Update these points as sales patterns change.

Restocking wisely means buying in bulk when you can get discounts, but not so much that you run out of cash. Use the 80/20 rule: 80% of your sales come from 20% of your items. Focus your restocking budget on those top items. For slow movers, buy smaller quantities more often. Also, negotiate with suppliers for credit terms or discounts on large orders. In many African markets, building a good relationship with your supplier can get you better prices and priority when stock is scarce.

Finally, keep a restock calendar. Mark when you place orders and when they arrive. This helps you plan cash flow and avoid stockouts during peak seasons like Christmas or Ramadan.

lessons.title: Managing Multiple Sales Channels
lessons.body:
Selling on multiple channelsâlike Jumia, Instagram, WhatsApp, and a physical stallâcan boost sales but also create inventory headaches. If you're not careful, you might sell the same item twice or oversell. The key is to centralise your inventory tracking.

Use a single master inventory list that all channels feed into. If you use inventory software (see Lesson 2), connect it to your online stores. For example, Zoho Inventory integrates with Shopify, WooCommerce, and Amazon. If you sell on Jumia, you can manually update stock after each sale, or use a third-party tool like Sellbrite. For WhatsApp and Instagram, you'll need to update manually, but do it immediately after each sale.

Set channel-specific rules. Some channels may have different pricing or shipping times. For example, on Jumia, you might offer free shipping, while on Instagram, you charge for delivery. Keep a spreadsheet that shows which items are listed on which channel. This prevents listing an item that's already sold out.

Allocate stock to channels if needed. If you have 10 units of a popular item and you're selling on three channels, you might reserve 4 for Jumia, 3 for Instagram, and 3 for walk-ins. This reduces the risk of overselling. But be flexibleâif one channel sells out, you can shift stock from another.

Communicate with your customers. If an item sells out on one channel, update the listing immediately. Apologise and offer alternatives or a refund. Bad reviews from overselling can hurt your reputation.

Finally, track performance per channel. Which channel brings the most sales? Which has the highest return rate? Use this data to decide where to focus your efforts. Maybe you'll drop a low-performing channel or invest more in ads on a high-performing one. Managing multiple channels is work, but with a central system, it's manageable and profitable.

lessons.title: Dealing with Dead Stock and Liquidation
lessons.body:
Dead stock is inventory that hasn't sold in 60-90 days. It ties up your cash and takes up space. Every reseller faces it, but you can minimise losses and recover some money. First, identify dead stock. Run a report from your inventory list: sort items by last sale date. Anything not sold in 3 months is dead. Also, check for items with low sales velocity.

Before liquidating, try to revive sales. Bundle dead items with popular ones. For example, if you have slow-moving phone cases, offer a 'case + charger' combo at a discount. Or run a flash sale on Instagram or WhatsApp: 'Clearance! 50% off selected items.' Promote to your existing customers via broadcast messages. Sometimes a simple price drop is enough.

If items still don't sell, consider liquidation. Options include: selling to other resellers at cost or below, donating to charity (for a tax write-off if applicable), or using online clearance platforms like Jumia Deals or OLX. You can also set up a 'mystery box'âcustomers pay a fixed price for a box of assorted items. This works well for small, varied goods.

For bulk liquidation, approach market traders or wholesalers. They may buy your entire dead stock at a steep discount (e.g., 30-50% of cost). It's better to recover something than nothing. If you're in a physical market, you can also swap dead stock with other traders for items you need.

Learn from dead stock. Why didn't it sell? Was it poor quality, wrong season, or bad marketing? Avoid repeating the mistake. In future, buy smaller quantities of new items and test demand before committing to bulk. Use pre-orders to gauge interest. Keep a 'lessons learned' log.

Finally, don't let dead stock sit forever. Set a deadline: if it doesn't sell by 90 days, liquidate. The cash you recover can be reinvested in better-selling products. Remember, cash flow is the lifeblood of your business.

quiz.q: What is the first step in organizing your inventory system?
quiz.explanation: Grouping products into categories makes it easier to assign codes and track items.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a recommended column in your master inventory list?
quiz.explanation: While supplier contact is useful, the master inventory list focuses on item details and stock levels.

quiz.q: How often should you do a physical count of your inventory?
quiz.explanation: Weekly physical counts help catch discrepancies early and keep records accurate.

quiz.q: What is a 'reorder point'?
options: A) The price at which you reorder
B) The minimum stock level that triggers a new order
C) The maximum stock you can hold
D) The time it takes to reorder
quiz.explanation: Reorder point is the stock level at which you place a new order to avoid stockouts.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label shelves and bins?
options: A) To make the space look pretty
B) To help you find items quickly and track inventory
quiz.explanation: Clear labeling speeds up picking and packing and reduces errors.

quiz.q: Which free inventory software is recommended for small businesses?
quiz.explanation: Zoho Inventory offers a free plan suitable for small resellers.

quiz.q: What should you do if you don't have reliable internet?
options: B) Use software that works offline and syncs later
C) Only use pen and paper
quiz.explanation: Offline-capable software allows you to record sales and update stock without constant internet.

quiz.q: How can inventory software help when selling on multiple channels?
options: B) It syncs stock across channels to prevent overselling
C) It delivers products for you
D) It creates ads for you
quiz.explanation: Syncing stock ensures you don't sell the same item on two channels.

quiz.q: What is a good backup method for your inventory data?
options: A) Keep it only on your phone
B) Save to Google Drive or USB weekly
D) Write it on a piece of paper and lose it
quiz.explanation: Regular backups protect your data from loss or theft.

quiz.q: Which of these is a threat to stored goods in many African cities?
quiz.explanation: Humidity and dust are common in many African regions and can damage inventory.

quiz.q: What is a good way to protect items from moisture?
options: C) Leave them in the sun
D) Wrap them in wet cloth
quiz.explanation: Silica gel absorbs moisture and helps prevent mold and rust.

quiz.q: Why should you use clear plastic bins for storage?
options: B) You can see contents without opening
quiz.explanation: Clear bins save time because you can identify items at a glance.

quiz.q: What packaging material is best for fragile items?
quiz.explanation: Bubble wrap provides cushioning to prevent breakage during shipping.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep your packing station organized?
options: B) To speed up order fulfilment and reduce errors
D) To hide items from thieves
quiz.explanation: An organized station means you can find supplies quickly and pack orders accurately.

quiz.q: What should you record in your sales log?
options: A) Only the total sales amount
B) Date, item code, quantity sold, price, and channel
quiz.explanation: Detailed sales records help you analyze performance and plan restocking.

quiz.q: What is sales velocity?
options: A) The speed of your internet
B) How many units of an item you sell per week on average
C) The price of an item
D) The time it takes to deliver
quiz.explanation: Sales velocity measures how quickly an item sells, which informs reorder points.

quiz.q: How do you calculate reorder point?
options: A) Average daily sales Ã lead time + safety stock
B) Total sales Ã· number of items
quiz.explanation: This formula ensures you order enough stock to cover lead time and unexpected demand.

quiz.q: What is the 80/20 rule in inventory?
options: A) 80% of sales come from 20% of items
B) 80% of items are dead stock
C) 80% of profit goes to tax
quiz.explanation: Focusing on the top 20% of items that generate 80% of sales maximizes profit.

quiz.q: Why is it important to build a good relationship with your supplier?
options: A) To get discounts and priority on stock
quiz.explanation: Good relationships can lead to better prices and first access to scarce items.

quiz.q: What is a restock calendar used for?
options: A) To plan when to place orders and expect deliveries
quiz.explanation: A restock calendar helps manage cash flow and avoid stockouts.

quiz.q: What is the main challenge of selling on multiple channels?
options: B) Inventory tracking and avoiding overselling
quiz.explanation: Without central tracking, you might sell the same item on two channels.

quiz.q: How can you centralize inventory across channels?
options: A) Use a single master inventory list or software
B) Keep separate lists for each channel
D) Only sell on one channel
quiz.explanation: A central system ensures all channels draw from the same stock data.

quiz.q: What is channel-specific allocation?
options: A) Reserving a certain quantity of stock for each sales channel
B) Setting different prices for each channel
C) Using different packaging for each channel
D) Hiring staff for each channel
quiz.explanation: Allocating stock to channels reduces the risk of overselling.

quiz.q: What should you do if an item sells out on one channel?
options: B) Update the listing immediately and inform customers
quiz.explanation: Updating listings prevents customer disappointment and bad reviews.

quiz.q: Why track performance per channel?
options: A) To decide where to focus marketing and resources
quiz.explanation: Channel performance data helps you allocate time and money effectively.

quiz.q: What is dead stock?
options: A) Items that haven't sold in 60-90 days
D) Items that are newly arrived
quiz.explanation: Dead stock ties up cash and space, so it needs to be managed.

quiz.q: What is a strategy to revive dead stock?
quiz.explanation: Bundling can make slow-moving items more attractive to customers.

quiz.q: Which of these is a liquidation option?
options: A) Selling to other resellers at a discount
quiz.explanation: All these methods can help recover some value from dead stock.

quiz.q: What is a 'mystery box'?
options: A) A box of assorted items sold at a fixed price
B) A box of new arrivals
C) A box of damaged goods
quiz.explanation: Mystery boxes are a fun way to clear small, varied dead stock.

quiz.q: What should you do to avoid dead stock in the future?
options: B) Test demand with small quantities and pre-orders
quiz.explanation: Testing demand reduces the risk of overstocking on items that don't sell.
